title: Clean Code Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Clean Code lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Write for the next reader
entries.summary: Code is read many times. A clear name explains the purpose of a value without making the reader solve a puzzle.
notes: A very short name is not always easier to understand.

entries.name: Name actions with verbs
entries.summary: Function names should explain what the action does. A reader should not need to inspect every line to understand a call.

example.code:
function addPrices(first, second) { return first + second; }
console.log(addPrices(3, 4));

notes: Avoid names such as doStuff that hide the purpose.

entries.name: Keep one job in a function
entries.summary: A small function with one clear job is easier to test and reuse. Separate a calculation from drawing a page.

example.code:
const totalPrice = prices => prices.reduce((sum, price) => sum + price, 0);
console.log(totalPrice([2, 3]));

notes: Do not mix a simple calculation with unrelated saving and navigation.

entries.name: Replace unexplained numbers
entries.summary: A named constant explains why a special value appears. It also gives the rule one clear place to change.
notes: Do not name every obvious arithmetic value; name values whose meaning needs explaining.

entries.name: Return early for simple cases
entries.summary: A guard clause handles a special case early. It can reduce deep nesting and make the main path easier to follow.
notes: Make sure an early return does not skip work that must always happen.

entries.name: Avoid needless repeated rules
entries.summary: When the same rule appears in several places, changes can be missed. Put a shared rule in one clear function.

example.code:
const passes = score => score >= 5;
console.log(passes(4), passes(7));

notes: Two similar lines do not always represent the same rule; do not combine unrelated ideas.

entries.name: Comments explain reasons
entries.summary: A useful comment explains why a choice was made. The code should already explain ordinary steps through names.
notes: Update comments when the code changes; a wrong comment misleads readers.

entries.name: Make errors helpful
entries.summary: An error should say what input was wrong or what action failed. It should not expose private details.
notes: Do not print secret values in error messages.

entries.name: Prefer clear conditions
entries.summary: A condition is easier to read when it states one clear question. Name a complicated condition if its purpose is not obvious.
notes: Be careful with double negatives such as notNotReady.

entries.name: Avoid surprising changes
entries.summary: A function that returns a new value can be easier to reason about than one that changes its input. Make changes clear in the function name or contract.
notes: sort changes its array, so copy first when the caller expects the original to stay.

entries.name: Refactor without changing behaviour
entries.summary: Refactoring improves the code structure while keeping the same intended behaviour. Tests help check that the behaviour stayed the same.
notes: Do not mix a large behaviour change with a readability-only change unless the scope is clear.

entries.name: Review a small change
entries.summary: A focused review checks whether a change solves its stated problem and keeps the code readable. Small changes are easier to inspect.

example.code:
const trimTitle = title => title.trim();
console.log(trimTitle("  Moon  ") === "Moon");

notes: Avoid unrelated rewrites while fixing one small issue.
